title: Computer Modern — Theorem & Definition Scaffold
description: A LaTeX-faithful lecture canvas for math-heavy content: a thin royal-blue-ruled definition box at top, italic serif theorem statement, and parenthesized numbered proof steps — every glyph set in Computer Modern, exactly as the TeX tradition demands.
philosophy: This template exists to remove every layer of decoration between a mathematician's reasoning and an audience's comprehension. It borrows its authority wholesale from half a century of LaTeX typesetting convention, refusing gradients, icon sets, and the rounded-corner visual vocabulary of modern slide builders. The speaker's credibility lives entirely in the rigour of the content; the design is structurally invisible. It is for chalkboard-and-projector rooms where the theorem is the event and the proof is the performance.
goodFor: Graduate-level mathematics and linear algebra lectures
MIT OCW-style open courseware slide exports
Conference talks built around theorem-proof-corollary structure
Courses where audience LaTeX fluency sets typographic expectations
avoidFor: Talks relying on photographic backdrops or icon-driven storytelling
Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews with dense data visualizations
Audiences unfamiliar with academic notation and proof conventions
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide carries the quiet authority of a printed journal frontmatter — spare, rectilinear, and unapologetic in its plainness. Composition breathes entirely through vertical white space; two hairline rules perform all structural division with no graphic ornament permitted. The mood is chalkboard-serious and institution-trusted, the kind of opening that signals the mathematics begins now. Avoid any softness, rounded forms, or decorative motif that competes with the austere typeset hierarchy.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid; all title content occupies cols 3–10, vertically centered with a slight upward pull to avoid optical heaviness. A single thin rule spans the full content width immediately above the title block, echoing the LaTeX beamer hairline-divider convention. Author name, affiliation, and date stack below the title with generous leading, separated by a second matching rule. No header band, no footer, no page number — the slide is structurally frameless.

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a high-resolution scan of a LaTeX-compiled handout projected in a dimly lit lecture theatre — austere, unhurried, and entirely without ornament. Compositional rhythm is top-weighted and columnar: the ruled definition box anchors authority at the crown, the italic theorem statement breathes below it as a formal declaration, and the proof steps descend in disciplined cadence like a choral response. The overall mood is one of rigorous economy — every element earns its space through logical necessity, not visual interest. Avoid any softness, iconography, illustrative metaphor, or decorative separation beyond a plain rule line.

  <rect width="1920" height="1080" fill="#f0f4f7"/>

  <!-- Definition box: full content width, delimited by top + bottom hairline -->

  <!-- Definition label + body -->
  <text x="135" y="170" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2a36" font-style="italic">Definition 3.4.</text>
  <text x="340" y="170" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" fill="#1f2a36">
    A sequence <tspan font-style="italic">(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="20">n</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">)</tspan><tspan baseline-shift="sub" font-size="20">n∈ℕ</tspan> in a metric space <tspan font-style="italic">(X, d)</tspan> is called a <tspan font-weight="700">Cauchy sequence</tspan> if for every
  </text>
  <text x="135" y="214" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" fill="#1f2a36">
    <tspan font-style="italic">ε > 0</tspan> there exists <tspan font-style="italic">N ∈ ℕ</tspan> such that <tspan font-style="italic">d(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="20">m</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">, x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="20">n</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">) < ε</tspan> whenever <tspan font-style="italic">m, n ≥ N</tspan>. The space <tspan font-style="italic">(X, d)</tspan> is <tspan font-weight="700">complete</tspan>
  </text>
  <text x="135" y="258" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" fill="#1f2a36">
    if every Cauchy sequence in <tspan font-style="italic">X</tspan> converges to a point of <tspan font-style="italic">X</tspan>.
  </text>

  <line x1="115" y1="290" x2="1805" y2="290" stroke="#1f2a36" stroke-width="1.2"/>

  <!-- Theorem statement in cols 2-11, italicised -->
  <text x="255" y="370" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="30" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2a36">Theorem 3.5 (Banach Fixed-Point Theorem).</text>
  <text x="255" y="418" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" font-style="italic" fill="#1f2a36">
    Let <tspan font-weight="700">(X, d)</tspan> be a non-empty complete metric space and let T : X → X be a contraction, i.e.
  </text>
  <text x="255" y="458" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" font-style="italic" fill="#1f2a36">
    there exists q ∈ [0, 1) with d(T x, T y) ≤ q · d(x, y) for all x, y ∈ X. Then T admits a
  </text>
  <text x="255" y="498" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" font-style="italic" fill="#1f2a36">
    unique fixed point x* ∈ X, and for every x₀ ∈ X the iteration xₙ₊₁ := T xₙ converges to x*.
  </text>

  <!-- Proof heading -->
  <text x="135" y="595" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="28" font-style="italic" fill="#1f2a36">Proof.</text>

  <!-- Numbered proof steps: numerals hang in col 1-2, prose in col 3-11 -->
  <!-- Step (1) -->
  <text x="135" y="650" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#5a8aa8">(1)</text>
  <text x="255" y="650" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#1f2a36">
    Fix <tspan font-style="italic">x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">0</tspan> ∈ <tspan font-style="italic">X</tspan> and set <tspan font-style="italic">x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n+1</tspan> := <tspan font-style="italic">T x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n</tspan>. By induction, <tspan font-style="italic">d(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n+1</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">, x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">) ≤ q</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="super" font-size="18">n</tspan> <tspan font-style="italic">d(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">1</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">, x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">0</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">)</tspan>.
  </text>

  <!-- Step (2) -->
  <text x="135" y="710" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#5a8aa8">(2)</text>
  <text x="255" y="710" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#1f2a36">
    For <tspan font-style="italic">m > n</tspan>, the triangle inequality yields <tspan font-style="italic">d(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">m</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">, x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">) ≤ q</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="super" font-size="18">n</tspan>(1 − <tspan font-style="italic">q</tspan>)<tspan baseline-shift="super" font-size="18">−1</tspan> <tspan font-style="italic">d(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">1</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">, x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">0</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">)</tspan>.
  </text>

  <!-- Step (3) -->
  <text x="135" y="770" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#5a8aa8">(3)</text>
  <text x="255" y="770" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#1f2a36">
    Since <tspan font-style="italic">q < 1</tspan>, the sequence <tspan font-style="italic">(x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n</tspan><tspan font-style="italic">)</tspan> is Cauchy; completeness of <tspan font-style="italic">X</tspan> supplies a limit <tspan font-style="italic">x*</tspan> ∈ <tspan font-style="italic">X</tspan>.
  </text>

  <!-- Step (4) -->
  <text x="135" y="830" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#5a8aa8">(4)</text>
  <text x="255" y="830" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#1f2a36">
    Contractions are Lipschitz, hence continuous: passing to the limit in <tspan font-style="italic">x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n+1</tspan> = <tspan font-style="italic">T x</tspan><tspan font-style="italic" baseline-shift="sub" font-size="18">n</tspan> gives <tspan font-style="italic">T x*</tspan> = <tspan font-style="italic">x*</tspan>.
  </text>

  <!-- Step (5) -->
  <text x="135" y="890" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#5a8aa8">(5)</text>
  <text x="255" y="890" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" font-size="26" fill="#1f2a36">
    If <tspan font-style="italic">y*</tspan> is another fixed point, <tspan font-style="italic">d(x*, y*) = d(T x*, T y*) ≤ q · d(x*, y*)</tspan>, forcing <tspan font-style="italic">x*</tspan> = <tspan font-style="italic">y*</tspan>.    ∎
  </text>

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with a 6% outer margin on all sides; no header band or decorative footer. The definition box occupies the full content width at the top, delimited only by a single thin rule above and below — no fill, no border radius. The theorem statement sits in cols 2–11, indented and italicised, separated from the definition box by roughly one line of vertical breathing room. Numbered proof steps cascade below: parenthesised step numerals hang in col 1–2 as a left-rail, prose or formulae occupy cols 3–11, each step separated by a consistent half-line gap. Slide number appears bottom-right in small roman numerals; nothing else occupies the footer zone.
